newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-AUSTRALIANS MAKE THEIR MARK AT WIMBLEDON.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-AUSTRALIANS MAKE THEIR MARK AT WIMBLEDON.

text.p: Doubles specialist Todd Woodbridge hoisted the Australian flag high over Wimbledon on Tuesday, but countryman Pat Cash's bid for a second helping of glory was stopped in its tracks.

It was Australia Day at Wimbledon with the country fielding 12 men in first round matches, the second highest representation at the grasscourt championships behind superpower United States with 14 players in the men's draw.

Woodbridge's epic five-set victory over American fifth seed Michael Chang in just under four hours on centre court was the highlight of their six victories. That figure could grow by one with Michael Tebbutt leading Spain's Javier Sanchez by two sets to one when fading light stopped play.
"I hope it's a resurgence," said Woodbridge after his victory over Chang. "Probably the years after Cashy (Cash) was winning provided an incentive. We all got a big kick out of him winning.
"I think when you get a Wimbledon champion that comes along, it boosts the juniors.
"Hopefully we can get another one right now to help keep pushing it further for the next generations."

Cash, who was critical of Wimbledon officials after being forced to qualify for the main draw, drew a boisterous crowd on court three, but they had to little to cheer after the 1987 winner took the first set.

The volatile Australian exchanged heated words with the chair umpire over a close line-call and there was plenty of head-shaking, but he failed to reignite the form which once carried him to the championship, losing in four sets.

The country's resurgence as a world tennis power began 12 months with Jason Stoltenberg's surprise semifinal berth at Wimbledon, continuing with rise in the world rankings of Mark Philippoussis and Patrick Rafter. They also have a Davis Cup semifinal showdown to look forward to against the United States in September.
Chang said his early exit coupled with Jim Courier's first round loss to German Michael Stich did not signal an end to U.S. dominance in tennis.
"I don't think you can really draw that conclusion with one particular tournament," he said.

Philippoussis, the highest ranked of the new Australian brigade at 13 in the world, was rated a fourth favourite to lift his first Grand Slam title by British bookmakers Ladbrokes before the start of the tournament.
Wimbledon officials also rated the tall Australian highly, seeding him seventh but on Tuesday he survived only 14 minutes to lose his rain delayed match against Britain's Greg Rusedski.
Rafter, seeded 12, also looked likely to make an early exit, but recovered from two sets down to beat South Africa's Grant Stafford.
Other winners included Stoltenberg, Todd Larkham, Sandon Stolle and Woodbridge's doubles partner Mark Woodforde.
Woodbridge said the likes of Rod Laver, Ken Rosewall, Roy Emerson and John Newcombe -- who headed Australia's charge in the 1960s and 70s -- had also been a strong influence in the country's rise.

"Having their influence that's really helped a lot with all the guys," said Woodbridge, who has failed to advance beyond the fourth round at grand slam tournament since making his professional debut in 1988.
